question: A simple model of human information processing describes information flowing through, in order:

options.text: Memory alone, with no role for attention or perception
Sensory receptors, attention, perception, memory, decision making, response selection and action
Action, then perception, then attention, which reverses the sequence in which a person must actually take in information before they can respond to any situation
Decision making before any sensory input is received

explanation: The standard stage model treats a person as processing information in a broadly ordered sequence — receiving a stimulus, attending to it, interpreting (perceiving) it, holding and comparing it against memory, deciding what to do, and then acting — though in practice stages can overlap and feed back on each other.

question: Attention is generally treated as a limited resource mainly because:

options.text: Humans can attend to an unlimited number of tasks simultaneously with no loss of performance
Attention has nothing to do with task performance, since every task a pilot performs is carried out by sensory channels that do not depend on any conscious choice at all and so cannot run short
Attention capacity increases without limit as more tasks are added
A person can only process a finite amount of information consciously at any one time, so attending fully to one thing reduces capacity available for another

explanation: Conscious attention has a finite capacity. Dividing it between tasks (divided attention) generally costs performance on at least one of them, which is why task prioritization and good workload management matter in a busy cockpit.

question: "Channelized attention" (sometimes called cognitive tunnelling) describes a state in which a person:

options.text: Distributes attention evenly across every available source of information
Becomes so absorbed in one task or problem that they fail to notice other important cues or instruments
Only occurs during routine, low-workload flight
Only occurs during routine, low-workload flight, when a pilot has spare capacity and is therefore free to notice every instrument and cue available in the cockpit

explanation: Channelized attention is a narrowing effect, often seen under high workload or stress, where focusing intently on a single problem (an unusual indication, a stuck switch) can mean other critical cues, including the aircraft's basic flight path, are missed.

question: Perception is not a passive recording of raw sensory data; it is better described as:

options.text: An active process in which the brain interprets incoming information using prior knowledge and expectation to construct a meaningful picture
Something that happens only after a decision has already been made
A process entirely independent of past experience, since each sense organ forms its picture afresh from the raw signal alone, without any reference to learned knowledge
An exact, unfiltered copy of whatever light or sound reaches the sense organs

explanation: The brain actively constructs a usable interpretation of incoming sensory data, filling gaps and resolving ambiguity using expectation and prior experience — which is exactly what makes perception fast and usually reliable, but also what makes it capable of being systematically fooled.

question: Because perception relies partly on expectation, a pilot who strongly expects a particular indication (for example, expecting the gear to be down because it usually is at this point) is at risk of:

options.text: Misreading an ambiguous or even contradictory indication as matching that expectation, rather than noticing the discrepancy
Being completely unaffected by expectation when reading an instrument
Perceiving only what is objectively true, regardless of expectation, which is an ideal that a pilot's brain can reach without any help from experience, training or prior knowledge
Automatically double-checking every indication without being prompted

explanation: Strong expectation can bias perception toward confirming what is anticipated, so a genuinely anomalous reading can be misread as normal — a mechanism behind many "it looked right so I didn't check again" errors, and part of why independent cross-checks matter.

question: Short-term (working) memory, compared with long-term memory, is characterized by:

options.text: A limited capacity and limited duration unless information is actively rehearsed or used
No role at all in everyday tasks such as copying a radio frequency, because every number a pilot hears is passed straight to long-term store without any delay or rehearsal
The ability to store skills and procedures permanently without any need for practice
No role at all in everyday tasks such as copying a radio frequency

explanation: Working memory can hold only a small number of items at once, and information fades from it within seconds unless it is rehearsed (repeated) or transferred into long-term memory — which is exactly why an ATC clearance can be forgotten if it is not written down or read back quickly.

question: A pilot who is given a long, complex ATC clearance with several changes in one transmission is at particular risk of:

options.text: Storing the clearance permanently in long-term memory automatically
Losing or confusing parts of it in working memory before it can be written down or read back, simply because its capacity is limited
Remembering every detail perfectly regardless of length
Having the information bypass working memory entirely, so that it is stored at once in long-term memory in its full form and needs no rehearsal or readback at all

explanation: Working memory's limited capacity means a long string of new information, especially several changed items at once, is prone to partial loss or confusion — a straightforward reason to write down, or ask for, a complex clearance rather than relying purely on memory.

question: Procedural memory, one category of long-term memory, stores:

options.text: Information that is lost within seconds, like working memory
Only facts and figures, never physical skills
Learned skills and sequences of action, such as how to fly a particular manoeuvre, often recalled without conscious step-by-step thought
Nothing that can be learned through practice, since a skill that has been repeated is never stored in any form that could be recalled later on in the flight

explanation: Procedural memory underlies well-practised skills — a trained pilot's stick-and-rudder inputs, a smooth checklist flow — which become largely automatic with practice, distinct from the more deliberate recall of facts stored in semantic memory.

question: A "motor programme" (a well-learned, practised motor skill) benefits performance mainly because once established, it:

options.text: Requires full conscious attention every time it is used, regardless of practice
Is always slower to execute than a newly learned skill
Can be executed with little conscious attention, freeing mental capacity for monitoring and decision making elsewhere
Cannot be disrupted by any distraction once learned, so a practised skill keeps working perfectly whatever the workload, the stress or the interruptions around it

explanation: A well-rehearsed motor programme runs with minimal conscious oversight, which is precisely what frees up limited attentional capacity for other demands — the trade-off is that a skill this automatic can sometimes run on without an intended trigger, which is part of how slip errors occur.

question: In the commonly used classification of human error, a "slip" is best described as:

options.text: Forgetting to carry out an intended action entirely
A plan or intention that was wrong from the start
A plan or intention that was wrong from the start, and which the pilot then carries out with full awareness that the chosen course of action is not the correct one
A correct intention carried out incorrectly — for example, intending to flip one switch but accidentally operating the adjacent one

explanation: A slip is an execution failure: the underlying plan was correct, but the action itself went wrong, often because a well-practised, largely automatic motor programme was triggered on the wrong target or at the wrong moment.

question: A "lapse", as distinct from a slip, is best described as:

options.text: An error that can only happen in writing, never in action, because the pilot's memory is always intact and only the written record of a planned sequence is ever at risk
An error that can only happen in writing, never in action
A memory failure — forgetting to carry out an intended action, or forgetting where one was in a sequence of steps
Executing an action correctly but with the wrong intention from the start

explanation: A lapse is about memory, not execution or planning: the intention was correct, but it was never carried out (or a place in a sequence was lost) because it slipped from memory — a classic example being forgetting a checklist item after an interruption.

question: A "mistake", in this classification, differs from a slip or a lapse because the problem lies in:

options.text: A problem that, by definition, cannot occur in experienced pilots
The physical execution of an otherwise correct plan
A simple failure of memory, since the mistake is always caused by forgetting a step that the pilot had originally intended and correctly planned to carry out later on
The plan or intention itself being wrong, even though it may then be carried out exactly as intended

explanation: A mistake is a planning-level error: the person forms an incorrect intention — based, for example, on a misdiagnosed situation or wrong assumption — and then may execute that flawed plan perfectly. This makes mistakes harder to catch through simple double-checking of execution alone.

question: Distinguishing between slips, lapses and mistakes is operationally useful mainly because:

options.text: The classification exists only for academic interest, with no practical use
Different error types call for different countermeasures — for example, physically separating similar-looking switches helps against slips, while better diagnosis training helps against mistakes
Only mistakes are preventable; slips and lapses cannot be reduced

Only mistakes are preventable; slips and lapses cannot be reduced, because they are caused by fatigue and by the natural limits of human memory, which no training, checklist or equipment design can change in any meaningful way

explanation: Because the underlying cause differs, the effective fix differs too: design changes (separated controls, better labelling) target slips; reminders, checklists and reducing interruptions target lapses; and improved training, procedures and diagnosis aids target mistakes.

question: A deliberate decision to depart from a known procedure, as distinct from a slip, lapse or mistake, is classified as:

options.text: A slip
A violation
An undesired aircraft state
A lapse

explanation: A violation is not an unintended failure at all — it is a conscious choice to deviate from a rule or procedure, whether out of necessity, habit or a belief that the rule does not apply, which sets it apart from the unintentional errors above.

question: Early in learning a new skill, a student pilot typically needs more conscious attention for each step than an experienced pilot does for the same manoeuvre, because:

options.text: Experienced pilots use a completely different part of the brain for the same task
New skills require less attention than practised ones, because a novice's attention is spread across fewer steps, so each one can be handled with a lighter load
The skill has not yet become an automatic motor programme, so each component still requires deliberate conscious control
Attention demand has nothing to do with the stage of learning

explanation: Practice is what converts a skill from a deliberate, attention-hungry sequence into a smoother, more automatic motor programme — which is why a new student finds a manoeuvre mentally taxing in a way an experienced pilot, doing the very same thing, does not.

question: A "mental schema" is best described as:

options.text: A physical structure located in the inner ear, which holds the balance receptors that tell the brain the position and movement of the head at every moment in flight
An organized structure of prior knowledge and expectations that helps a person interpret new information quickly
A single isolated fact with no connection to other knowledge
A term used only in relation to motor skills, never to perception

explanation: A schema is a mental framework built from past experience that lets new information be interpreted efficiently by fitting it into an existing structure, rather than every new situation being analysed completely from scratch.

question: A pilot's schema built from years of flying one type of approach can become a liability when:

options.text: Schemas, by definition, can never be applied incorrectly
The approach is entirely routine and matches the schema exactly
An unusual approach genuinely differs from the pattern the schema expects, and the pilot applies the familiar pattern instead of recognising the real difference
The pilot has never flown that type of approach before, so no schema has yet been built for it, and the pilot must rely on the written procedure and direct observation alone

explanation: The very efficiency that makes a schema useful — filling in gaps automatically based on past pattern — can mislead a pilot into treating a genuinely unusual situation as if it were the familiar one it resembles, overriding cues that the present case is actually different.

question: When several possible responses to a situation seem plausible, the time taken to select and begin one of them (response selection) generally:

options.text: Decreases as the number of choices increases
Increases as the number of plausible choices increases
Is completely unaffected by the number of choices available
Is always instantaneous regardless of complexity

explanation: Choosing among more options generally takes longer than choosing among fewer, well-established options — a consideration behind designing emergency procedures to narrow down to a clear, limited set of actions rather than an open-ended menu of possibilities.

question: Feedback on the outcome of an action (for example, confirming that a switch moved to the position intended) matters in the information-processing model because it:

options.text: Always arrives before the action it refers to
Has no role once an action has been taken, because the outcome of a completed action is already fixed and cannot be changed by any information that arrives later on
Is only relevant to automated systems, not to human actions
Allows the person to confirm the action had the intended effect, or to detect and correct an error before it has further consequences

explanation: Feedback closes the loop between intention and outcome. Without it, a slip (operating the wrong switch, say) could go completely unnoticed; good feedback — a visible switch position, an aural tone, a readback — gives a person the chance to catch and correct their own error.

question: Human reliability, in the sense used when discussing error generation, is best understood as:

options.text: Generally high but never perfect, so systems and procedures should be designed assuming errors will sometimes occur rather than assuming they will not

Completely unpredictable and therefore impossible to design against, since no pattern in human behaviour can be recorded, measured or anticipated by the designers of any flight deck system in use today
Completely unpredictable and therefore impossible to design against
Irrelevant to aircraft design, which only needs to consider mechanical reliability

explanation: No amount of training eliminates the possibility of human error entirely. Good system and procedure design, following this view of human reliability, builds in ways to catch and trap likely errors rather than relying solely on people never making one.

question: "Sustained attention" (vigilance) over a long, low-event monitoring task, such as a long cruise with an autopilot engaged, is well known to:

options.text: Only apply to visual tasks, never to monitoring sounds or alerts
Improve steadily the longer the monitoring continues, because a person settles into the task and becomes more alert to subtle changes the longer they watch the display in front of them
Stay perfectly constant regardless of how long the task lasts
Decline over time, making a person less likely to notice an infrequent, unexpected event the longer the monitoring period continues

explanation: Vigilance tends to decay over a prolonged, low-stimulation monitoring task — a well-documented effect that is part of why automation and procedures build in active cross-checks and alerts rather than relying purely on sustained human watchfulness over long, uneventful periods.

question: Confirmation bias, as it applies to in-flight decision making, describes the tendency to:

options.text: Change one's mind immediately upon encountering any contradictory evidence
Notice and weight information that supports an existing belief more heavily than information that contradicts it
Only occur in people with little flying experience, since experienced pilots are trained to weigh every new fact equally and so are never affected by a prior belief at all
Treat all new information with exactly equal weight regardless of an existing belief

explanation: Once a belief about the situation is formed — "that noise is probably normal", say — confirmation bias tends to make supporting evidence stand out while contradicting evidence is discounted or missed, which can delay recognising that the original belief was wrong.

question: An interruption during a checklist (such as a radio call partway through) is a well-known trigger for which type of error?

options.text: A lapse, where the checklist item after the interruption is forgotten or skipped
A violation, because procedures were deliberately disregarded
A mistake, because the overall plan for the checklist was wrong
An error that cannot occur once a checklist has started, because a checklist that has begun is protected from every form of interruption by its own structure and sequence

explanation: An interruption disrupts the place-keeping that a sequential task like a checklist relies on, making it easy to resume at the wrong point or skip a step — a classic memory-based lapse rather than a flawed plan or a deliberate shortcut.

question: A checklist, read aloud and physically touched item by item, helps reduce error mainly by:

options.text: Working only by coincidence, with no link to how information processing actually works
Forcing deliberate, conscious attention onto each item rather than relying on an automatic motor programme or memory alone
Eliminating the possibility of any error whatsoever
Replacing the need for any training at all, since a checklist that is read aloud and touched item by item makes any prior knowledge of the aircraft and its systems unnecessary

explanation: A spoken, touched checklist pulls each item back into conscious, deliberate processing instead of leaving it to habit or memory alone, directly countering the slips and lapses that purely automatic or memory-based performance is prone to.
